verdicts.reading: 'These truly personal computers' are the body-worn and carried devices of the preceding sentences (claims 003-005: 'a dozen computers on and around their bodies'). They are mostly solid-state with electronic memory.
verdicts.reason: The sentence follows the body-LAN sentence and says 'these truly personal computers', so the referent is the small carried devices, not notebooks. In 2009 phones and smartphones used flash memory only, and most music players were flash (nano, shuffle, touch). This meets the device test (more than 50% of new units). Notebooks still used hard disks, but the text does not refer to them. Grader B's notebook reading is less faithful to the antecedent.

verdicts.reading: Molecular-scale machines with their own computational control have been demonstrated in the lab, and nanoengineering is not yet practical.
verdicts.reason: Grader B says no such device existed by 2009. That is wrong. Benenson and Shapiro demonstrated a programmable autonomous molecular computer in 2001 and in 2004 an autonomous DNA automaton that evaluated cancer-gene expression and on its own released an antisense drug molecule. Autonomous DNA walkers were shown in 2003-2004. Nanoengineering was not a practical technology in 2009. Both halves hold. The devices are molecular, not Drexler-style atom-by-atom assemblers; the text's 'molecule by molecule' covers them.

verdicts.reading: Computers are central across teaching, administration and learning in schools, as elsewhere.
verdicts.reason: Routine-use test: more than 20% of the relevant industry. In 2009, 94% of US public school teachers used grading systems, 96% word processing and 94% the internet for instruction or administration; 97% of schools had classroom computers. 'All facets' is an overstatement, but routine use far above the 20% threshold across teaching and administration meets the rule. B's 'computer-centred instruction' test adds a condition the text does not state.

verdicts.reading: Two trends: paper document output is falling, and old print is being scanned at a fast rate. The claim states a process ('being rapidly scanned'), not completion.
verdicts.reason: Both trends were real by 2009. World printing and writing paper production peaked in 2007 at about 120 Mt and fell in 2008-2009, and has not regained the peak. Google had scanned about 7 million books by November 2008 and 12 million by June 2010. Grader A tested completion (share of all titles scanned), but the text claims a rate, not completion.

verdicts.reading: Most students own a personal thin tablet under one pound with a high-resolution display.
verdicts.reason: In 2009 the share was near zero, so no hit and no 'measurable by 2009' partial. The question is the 3-5 year window. Sub-pound high-resolution tablets arrived in 2012-2013 (iPad mini 0.68 lb, Nexus 7, Kindle Fire HD). Pearson's 2013 survey found about three in ten US students in grades 4-12 owned a tablet, with younger students more likely; 42% of high-school students used tablets regularly in 2014. A large part of the tablets children owned were 7-8 inch models under a pound. This puts ownership of a matching device near the 20% line in 2013-2014. Grader A's claim of under 5% by 2014 is not supported. Low certainty: no source splits student tablet ownership by weight.

verdicts.reason: The text says materials 'are accessed through wireless communication'; it does not say 'mainly'. In the sentence, GPS attaches most naturally to 'finding their way around'; separate electronic obstacle aids also existed. verdicts.reading: The underclass is not a disruptive political force; public assistance and general affluence contain it.
verdicts.reason: The observable state held: the poor did not form a significant political movement in 2009-2011, and public assistance expanded (ARRA raised SNAP benefits from April 2009; participation peaked at 47.6 million in 2013). Occupy (2011) was not an underclass movement. The mechanism cannot be tested, but no faithful reading gives a miss on the observable state. Low-to-medium certainty.

Responsive improvising partners stayed in research labs, so 'routinely jam' with responsive musicians was not mainstream by 2014. Measurable but below mainstream gives partial. verdicts.reading: Two readings. Reading 1: confidence among AGI-oriented researchers that machines will pass the Turing test by about 2019-2029 is growing. Reading 2: confidence among AI researchers and the public in general is growing.
verdicts.reason: The first clause (computers still fail) is true. The forecast is the trend in confidence, and the text does not say whose. The only survey (AGI-09, self-selected optimists) supports reading 1; mainstream AI opinion of the period was more sceptical, and the 2002 Kapor-Kurzweil bet framed the question as open. No series measures a change in confidence between 1999 and 2009. Neither reading dominates, the readings point to different verdicts, and the trend itself has no measure.
